title: Multistage stochastic optimization via kernels
contribution: Represents multistage decision rules with side information as elements of a reproducing kernel Hilbert space, trains them by functional SGD with kernel-OMP pruning (SMOK), proves asymptotic optimality, and finds sparse, fast, near-optimal rules on synthetic inventory and shipment problems.
problem_entry: {DA SD; ML as engine} Multistage stochastic optimization with side information, where decisions do not affect the uncertainty (p. 1); the entry is the group's own limits: SRO and SRO-knn need scenario trees and hours for a few stages (p. 2), local kernel methods need more data (p. 3), and the Bertsimas-Koduri kernel formulation grows cubically with the data (pp. 3-4).
key_idea: Decision rules as RKHS elements with covariate-augmented domains (p. 5), trained by functional SGD on the regularized empirical loss (pp. 6-8), with kernel orthogonal matching pursuit pruning the dictionary after every step to Hilbert-norm tolerance epsilon (Algorithms 1-2, pp. 9-11); a global learned rule instead of reweighted samples or linear rules over uncertainty sets (pp. 2-3).
assumptions: Convex loss, i.i.d. sample paths, no cross-stage correlation assumption (pp. 2, 6); compact data space with bounded universal kernels, Lipschitz loss, convexity and differentiability (A1-A3, p. 11); constraints only via a quadratic penalty, feasibility not guaranteed (p. 14); synthetic inventory data and a reproduced synthetic shipment problem (pp. 15, 20).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: constant step eta and pruning tolerance P2*eta^2 give expected excess regularized loss O(eta/lambda) (p. 12)
Corollary 1: eta = sqrt(P1/N), lambda -> 0, lambda*sqrt(N) -> infinity give L1 convergence to the optimum over continuous rules, rate O(1/(lambda*sqrt(N))) (p. 12)
SGD descent inequality with the projection error entering as a bias of order epsilon (Lemma 6, p. 29); penalty feasibility as psi -> infinity (Lemma 7, p. 30)
dictionary size bounded by a covering number depending on eta and P2 but not N: worst-case O(NM^3) time and O(NM^2) space vs Omega(N^2) unpruned; covering number unknown in closed form (pp. 12-13)
analytic lower bound for T <= 5: drop the two loose bound constraints and solve the rest with the newsvendor fractile under normal noise (Appendix D, pp. 31-32)
experiments: Python/NumPy on a 4-core laptop (p. 15); 10-period inventory with N = 2,000: SMOK loss 491.30 in 0.3 h with 1.5e3 parameters vs MOK 493.74 (0.1 h) and SAA-knn 496.04 (14.36 h), SRO intractable (Table 1, p. 16); near the lower bounds and far better than affine rules in sweeps (pp. 16-19); shipment planning: MOK best profit, SMOK second, SMOK time flat at 150-260 s but SAA-knn fastest (Tables 2-3, p. 21); all data synthetic.
positioning: Against local kernel predict-then-optimize methods (Hanasusanto-Kuhn, Pflug-Pichler) and predictive-only online kernel learning; follows Koppel et al. (2016) for pruned FSGD; extends the group's SRO, SRO-knn and Bertsimas-Koduri kernel work (pp. 2-4).
writing: Four numbered contributions with a 'to the best of our knowledge' first-tractable claim (p. 4); experiments narrated figure by figure; two SMOK/MOK label slips (pp. 17-18).
limits_future: Decisions must not affect the uncertainty (pp. 1, 21); penalty-only feasibility (p. 14); unknown covering number (p. 13); constant step trades accuracy for memory (p. 12); no future-work list (pp. 21-22).

method_links.note: Decisions scored out of sample (loss, profit), but baselines are the group's own SRO, SRO-knn, SAA-knn and textbook affine rules on synthetic data, not an owner's rule; step 4 varied: the decision rule itself is learned globally rather than ML weights inside a sample average.
Certificate idea moved out of MIO: an optimality gap against an analytic lower bound that exists only because the generator is known, and only for T <= 5.
A scenario-tree problem rewritten as kernel learning rather than LP or MIO; tractability by pruning, not by a class-keeping device; boundary printed (penalized constraints, unknown covering number).

On synthetic instances, build a lower bound from the known generator (drop non-binding constraints, solve the rest in closed form) and report gaps (pp. 31-32).

title: Robust Regression over Averaged Uncertainty
contribution: Averaging the squared loss uniformly over a symmetric uncertainty set, instead of taking its worst case, yields exactly ridge regression with a closed-form lambda for l_p sets (and asymptotically for Schatten balls) but not for non-symmetric polytopes; on UCI and synthetic data it beats worst-case robust regression by under 1% MSE.
problem_entry: {ML RO} The group's worst-case equivalence gives root-mean-square regression, 'not practically used', while practice solves least squares (pp. 2, 9); worst case can be too conservative (p. 8); no exact regularization strengths for the least-squares case (p. 2).
key_idea: Integrate the loss over the set (Definition 1, a uniform-distribution stochastic program, p. 9); the exact second-order expansion (Lemma 12, p. 17) and symmetry kill the linear term (Corollaries 1-3, pp. 12-13), leaving ridge with lambda equal to the set's second moment (p. 18).
assumptions: Linear regression with additive feature perturbations uniform on ellipsoidal, box, diamond, budget, Schatten or polytopal sets, no data model beyond the set (pp. 7-8); ten UCI sets with hit-and-run perturbations at six levels and 10 seeds, 80/20 split (pp. 21-22); synthetic 300-900 samples, 3-10 informative features, 20 seeds (p. 24).
proof_devices: odd-function integrals vanish over symmetric sets (Lemma 5, Corollaries 1-3, pp. 12-13)
exact second-order expansion of the squared loss in the perturbation (Lemma 12, p. 17)
Theorem 6: closed-form lambda, box n*rho^2/3, diamond 2n*rho^2/((nk+2)(nk+1)), budget two-term expression valid for sqrt(2)/2*rho <= Gamma <= rho (pp. 18-19)
Theorem 7: Schatten balls via isotropic constants, asymptotic and square only (p. 19; Remark p. 12); Theorem 8: non-symmetric polytopes keep a linear term, no ridge (p. 20)
volumes by Coxeter's formula and corner truncation (Lemmas 2-3, pp. 11-12); simplex integration formulas for polytopes (pp. 15-16)

my reading: ellipsoid constant printed as 1/k in the statement and via V(nk, rho) in the proof (p. 18), not scaling as rho^2; general step gives n*rho^2/(nk+2) (my computation); budget radii swapped between definition (4) and Lemma 3's proof and validity range (pp. 7, 12, 19)
experiments: Gurobi, Julia 1.9.3, Python 3.10.6, barrier, public code (p. 21); 2,400 real-data runs: AUR beats WUR by 0.4-0.9% MSE on average, rising with perturbation, box set excepted (p. 22); theorem lambda beats CV lambda by 0.6-0.8% and CV selects up to six different lambda across seeds (Table 2, pp. 22-23); synthetic gains shrink with samples and informative features (p. 24); no dispersion, tests or run-time numbers.
positioning: Starts from the group's worst-case equivalence (Bertsimas-Copenhaver; Bertsimas-Brown et al.) and sets itself against DRO equivalences (Blanchet et al.; martingale DRO) as a deterministic alternative (pp. 3-4, 9-10).
writing: Contribution bullets stress 'exact, closed-form, in some cases analytical' solutions (p. 4); empirical claims phrased universally in the conclusion (p. 25) with the box-set exception noted only in the body (p. 22).
limits_future: Equivalence fails for non-symmetric sets (p. 20); Schatten results asymptotic and square only (p. 12); AUR needs a larger lambda (p. 25); future: matrix regression, RO with solution constraints, discrete RO (p. 26).

method_links.note: Ridge regression, owned by statistics, written exactly as an averaged robust problem; symmetry plus the set's second moment is the class-keeping device; boundary printed (non-symmetric polytopes, asymptotic Schatten). Also Heuristic 1 evidence: the procedure practice runs is shown to solve a robust problem exactly.

Conservatism answered by averaging instead of a budget; the knob rho maps to lambda in closed form, independent of the solution, and replaces cross-validation; no probability bound and no price curve.

new_pattern_candidates.evidence: Ridge regression equals averaged robust regression for every symmetric set considered, with lambda in closed form; the equivalence fails for non-symmetric polytopes.

For increasing noise levels from nested sets, require samples at a higher level to lie outside the smaller set (p. 24).

title: Adaptive pricing in unit commitment under load and capacity uncertainty
contribution: Proposes adaptive pay-as-bid and uniform pricing for adaptive robust unit commitment with load and capacity uncertainty, read off the dual of the linear-decision-rule robust counterpart with binaries fixed; proves the schemes coincide and deter self-scheduling when the worst case is realized, and illustrates them on two textbook examples.
problem_entry: {RO AP; LO duality; IO with commitments fixed} ARO and stochastic UC already adapt commitment and dispatch, but ISO marginal and convex-hull prices are deterministic and need ad hoc uplifts that motivate self-scheduling; only two prior papers price robust UC, neither with ARO (pp. 1-2).
key_idea: ARO-UC with linear decision rules over norm-ball load and capacity sets (pp. 2-3); fix binaries at the optimum as in O'Neill et al.'s IP pricing and price from the robust dual (p. 3); day-ahead payments for commitment and non-adaptive dispatch, adaptive part as an upper bound on intra-day payments, plus payments proportional to the uncertainty-set sizes (p. 4).
assumptions: Scarf-type UC; l1, l2, l-infinity sets whose sizes control conservativeness (p. 2); non-adaptive dispatch tied to expected load (p. 3); LDR may not be optimal (p. 2); binaries fixed for pricing (p. 3); data: Scarf example and Chen et al.'s two-generator three-hour example, no ISO data (pp. 7, 9).
proof_devices: Theorem 1: day-ahead pay-as-bid equals uniform price plus uplift, by complementary slackness between the robust problem and its dual (p. 4)
Theorem 2: total payments coincide when the worst case is realized (p. 5)
Theorem 3: no generator gains by self-scheduling in its own robust problem under centralized prices, at the worst-case realization (pp. 5-6)
dual-norm robust counterparts give the prices and the uncertainty-size payments (pp. 3-4)
experiments: Worked examples, no solver or timings: Scarf deterministic $260 vs ARO payments $328.5 (identical under both schemes), $352 with capacity uncertainty (pp. 7-8); intra-day cost below the adaptive part, equal at the worst case (Fig. 1, p. 8); Chen et al.: convex-hull $365 duality-gap uplift vs ARO with none (p. 9); text says $280 against a printed $260 and adaptive uplifts total 208.5 vs 180 (p. 7, my arithmetic).
positioning: Against ISO marginal (IP) pricing and convex-hull pricing (O'Neill et al.; Hua-Baldick; the group's own Dantzig-Wolfe convex-hull paper); notes only two earlier robust-UC pricing papers, neither ARO (p. 1).
writing: The abstract's 'two major disadvantages' framing is repeated in the introduction (p. 1); 'the first' claimed in the abstract and the conclusion (pp. 1, 10); theory, then worked examples with full payment tables.
limits_future: Uplifts remain in the uniform scheme though fixed day-ahead (pp. 4, 7); guarantees only at the worst-case realization (pp. 5-6); LDR and fixed binaries (pp. 2-3); small examples; no future-work statement (p. 10).

method_links.note: Class kept by linear decision rules and norm-ball sets; prices and uplifts read off the dual (step 4); boundary printed only in part (LDR may be suboptimal; theorems at the worst case).
Set sizes are the knobs and the uncertainty is priced, but the cost of protection appears at single points ($260 to $328.5 to $352; $7340 to $7860), with no curve and no probabilistic bound.
The owners' current pricing rules are the comparators, but only on textbook examples, without ISO data or field test, unlike the ISO New England evaluation of the 2012 ARO-UC paper.

title: Renalase Identified by Machine Learning Methods As A Novel Independent Predictor Of Mortality In Hospitalized Patients With COVID-19
contribution: A Yale-led single-centre COVID-19 cohort study (437 patients) in which a priori and stepwise logistic regression and XGBoost with SHAP all retain low serum renalase as a predictor of 180-day mortality; XGBoost reaches test AUC 0.85.
problem_entry: {AP ML} Identify traditional and novel predictors of mortality in hospitalized COVID-19 patients and test whether low renalase predicts independently (pp. 3-4); traditional predictor models have predictable biases and validate poorly, ML may generalize better (p. 4).
key_idea: Three-model triangulation: a priori logistic regression as baseline, backward-stepwise logistic regression and XGBoost with SHAP; renalase called independent because it appears in all three (pp. 6, 8); no optimization model, post-hoc interpretability (p. 6).
assumptions: Single-centre retrospective cohort, March-June 2020: 437 analysed of 473 enrolled (3,450 admitted), 71 deaths, 897 samples (pp. 3, 7); features with >30% missing dropped, OptImpute for the rest, cut-offs by quantiles and clinical judgement (p. 5); 50/20/30 split, 200 random splits for CIs (p. 6).
proof_devices: n/a: no formulation or proofs; univariate Fisher and chi-square tests and quartile-trajectory comparisons (pp. 5, 8-9)
experiments: Test AUC: a priori LR 0.72, backward LR 0.70, XGBoost 0.85 (Table 3, p. 18), though the abstract and one discussion line say 0.87 (pp. 3, 9); train and validation AUC of 1 for XGBoost and backward LR undiscussed (p. 18); Table 2 repeats rows for IFN-alpha/IFN-lambda and IL-6/TNF-alpha (p. 18, my reading).
positioning: Clinical COVID-19 biomarker literature (cytokines, cardiac markers) and the team's own earlier renalase cohort; ML justified by a 13-algorithm bioinformatics benchmark (pp. 3-6).
writing: Clinical IMRaD format; headline AUC inconsistent between abstract and table (pp. 3, 18); 'independent predictor' used for consistency across models (p. 8).
limits_future: Single site, first wave, pre-vaccination, few serial samples (p. 11); future prospective studies and a possible therapeutic role for exogenous renalase (p. 11); last author's renalase patents and equity declared (pp. 2, 11-12).

method_links.note: The field's traditional model is the explicit baseline, but predictions are scored (AUC, PR-AUC, calibration) with no decision attached (Warning sign 4); prospective validation deferred.

A held-out duel against the incumbent model, but no exact model: a boosted ensemble wins with post-hoc SHAP while the group's interpretable learners (OCT) are absent, in tension with Taste mark 5 (my reading); perfect training AUCs unremarked.

title: Hospital-wide inpatient flow optimization
contribution: HIFO: a three-horizon mixed-integer bed-assignment model for a whole hospital, fed by ML predictions and protected by prediction-based adaptive robust optimization, re-solved every two hours; solved in seconds for a 600-bed hospital and, in historical replay, cutting boarding delays and off-service placements against staff decisions.
problem_entry: {AP DA RO; IO and ML as engines} Hospital-wide coordination is wanted (p. 2), but patient-level bed-assignment models are myopic or slow (12+ hours for 96 beds) and unit-level queueing/MDP models miss patient requirements (pp. 4, 6-8).
key_idea: Granularity matched to horizon: patient assignments now, unit flows in 2-hour periods to 6 am, hospital capacity for the week, coupled and weighted by lambda and lambda_w (Table 2, pp. 9-12); single-move assumption links aggregates to individuals (p. 10); ML predictions from risk scores (pp. 14-16) wrapped in an uncertainty set (pp. 16-17) with static or affine rules (pp. 21-22); closed-loop re-solve (p. 12).
assumptions: ~600 beds, 31 units, 15 services (pp. 3-4); ~18,000 binaries and 630 constraints (p. 9); single-move assumption validated at >85% (p. 10); piecewise-linear convex costs calibrated with the partner (pp. 11, 13); scheduled admissions certain (p. 16); independent Poisson flows for Proposition 1, relaxed to independent patients (pp. 19-20); data January-August 2019 (p. 23).
proof_devices: Proposition 1: P(realized cost >= robust cost) <= exp(-(c_bar/c_inf) Gamma_c^2/(1+Gamma_c)) for a fixed flow, a posteriori, reading the worst case as a value-at-risk bound (p. 19)
new large-deviation bound for sums of independent Poisson variables (Lemma 1, Appendix A.1; cited p. 19)
guarantee for open-loop day-level flows only; closed loop left open (p. 20)
epigraph plus constraint-wise robustification for the robust counterpart (p. 21)
full affine rules intractable, so affine with known recourse (Proposition 1 still holds) and restricted affine (p. 22)
experiments: Hybrid historical replay from recorded states with staff decisions between runs (p. 23); vs history, fluid and SAA-100 (p. 24); median solves 0.36-0.70 s, 99th percentile up to 41.2 s (Table 4, p. 25); 1-day runs cut waiting 20%/11% and off-service 6%, 7-day runs 35%/18%/24% (p. 26); census +0.9-2.6%, transfers -12.9% on 1-day runs (Table 5, p. 28); 38% of patients better, 20% worse (p. 28); 20% compliance keeps ~70% of the off-service gain (p. 29); solver and hardware not named in the text read.
positioning: Between patient-level bed-assignment models (Thompson et al.; Thomas et al.; Schafer et al.) and unit-level queueing/MDP models (Kilinc et al.; Dai-Shi); RO chosen over stochastic and DRO modelling for tractability and a value-at-risk reading (pp. 4-8, 17-20).
writing: 'One of the most comprehensive of its kind' (p. 4); 7-day headline numbers in the abstract, caveats on PACU, compliance and fairness in the body (pp. 2, 26-29).
limits_future: Single-move assumption, implicit costs, no model of decisions changing flows (pp. 12-13); PACU gain to be taken with a pinch of salt (pp. 26-27); full compliance assumed (p. 28); future: real pilot, closed-loop theory, adjustable DRO, fairness and behaviour (p. 29).

method_links.note: Owner, decision, EHR data and the historical staff rule as baseline; decision metrics with census and volume controls; costs set with the partner; compliance curve; field test deferred with smaller real gains predicted. Also Heuristic 4 evidence: PACU caveat, fewer transfers, 20% of patients worse printed in the body.

Granularity matched to horizon plus the single-move assumption keep a 600-bed hospital in an MIO solved in seconds; boundary printed (full affine rules intractable; guarantees for open-loop flows only).

lambda and lambda_w trace a waiting/off-service frontier with the chosen point marked, and compliance p traces a second curve; but the probabilistic bound is solution-specific (a posteriori), not solution-independent.

title: A machine learning approach to two-stage adaptive robust optimization
contribution: Learns the strategies of two-stage ARO (binary first-stage decision, worst-case extreme point, second-stage tight constraints) from CCG-solved instances with XGBoost or Optimal Policy Trees, plus learned warm starts and class merging, giving millisecond solutions with high accuracy on small parametric families.
problem_entry: {RO DA; IO for binary first-stage decisions, ML} Two-stage ARO is heavy: affine rules have no near-optimality or feasibility guarantee and exact methods may not scale (p. 2); CCG's unit-commitment solve time jumps at n = 5 on the authors' machine (Fig. 1, pp. 7-8); real-time uses need milliseconds (p. 2); the group's strategy learning for MICO does not carry over directly (p. 2).
key_idea: Encode solutions as three finite strategies (decision; decision plus worst-case extreme point; decision plus tight constraints) (pp. 9-10); sample the parameter in a ball, solve by CCG, train XGBoost or OPT on reward matrices (pp. 10-12); online, predict and solve only the reduced LP (p. 10); extensions for varying dimensions, learned warm starts and fixing, and class merging (pp. 14-19).
assumptions: Fixed recourse, affine dependence on d, polyhedral sets so worst cases are extreme points (pp. 4-5); labels near-optimal only, from an alternating-direction heuristic with three starts (p. 5; Remark 1, p. 10); parameters sampled from small balls around fixed centres (Remark 2, p. 10; pp. 20-21); facility location, inventory control and Carrion-Arroyo unit commitment (pp. 20-21).
proof_devices: no theorems; CCG on the extreme-point reformulation with a heuristic max-min oracle (pp. 4-6)
per-prediction infeasibility and relative suboptimality against the heuristic second-stage evaluation (pp. 9-10)
warm-start/fixing threshold p chosen as the smallest value with validation misclassification below a bound (p. 16)
rare tight-constraint sets merged into a union so the reduced LP still contains each instance's tight set (pp. 17-19)
experiments: Julia 1.4.1, Gurobi, a 2.6 GHz laptop, OPT from Interpretable AI (pp. 7, 20); 70/30 split (p. 22); near-optimal labels: accuracy >= 0.93, never infeasible, max suboptimality <= 0.001, speed-ups up to 3.37 million (pp. 22-25); large UC with loose labels: accuracy 0.18, max suboptimality 0.0205, speed-up 8.49e7 (Table 12, pp. 27-28); Algorithm 6 >10x faster data generation (p. 28); offline time only in the Supplementary Material (p. 20).
positioning: Extends the group's learning-to-optimize line (Bertsimas-Stellato 2021, 2022; Bertsimas-Kim 2023) to ARO; against affine rules and exact ARO algorithms (CCG, Benders, scenario reduction, branch-and-bound, Fourier-Motzkin) (pp. 2-3).
writing: 'The first' ML approach to ARO claimed (p. 2); the headline speed-up of more than 10 million times (p. 3) comes from the setting with 0.18 accuracy (p. 28); results as bullet lists under each table.
limits_future: Heavy offline phase (p. 2); suboptimal labels from CCG (pp. 5, 10); many classes for large uncertainty sets (p. 17); no future-work list (p. 29).

method_links.note: Learned predictions warm-start or fix binaries and every prediction carries infeasibility and maximum suboptimality, but the yardstick is uncertified (heuristic inner solver) and the duel is a speed race with CCG. Also Heuristic 5 evidence: a repeatedly solved optimization has its strategy learned offline.
The price of interpretability measured by running OPT against XGBoost: a two-point price with no knob curve or bound.
The learning-to-optimize line passes from Stellato to Kim, and the prescriptive learner comes from the group's company Interpretable AI.
